toc.title: Responsibility, root user, identities, policies, roles, federation and directories

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Apply security best practices to the root user and IAM users
  • Design an authorization model with users, groups, roles and policies
  • Design role-based access with AWS STS, role switching and cross-account access
  • Design a multi-account security strategy with Organizations, SCPs and Control Tower
  • Decide when to federate a directory service with IAM roles

2Responsibility, root user, identities, policies, roles, federation and directories

Running case

Lantern and Loom Opens the Doors

  • The founder still signs in as the root user
  • Eight engineers now share the account, and a partner photo studio must upload images
  • Development, test and production will soon live in separate accounts
  • Staff already sign in to company systems with an existing directory
  • Your job: decide who gets which access, with the least privilege that works

The Shared Responsibility Model

AWS: security of the cloud You: security in the cloud
Covers The hardware, software, networking and facilities that run the services Your data, identities and permissions, and the settings of the services you choose
Example Physical security of the data centers IAM permissions, encryption choices, guest OS patches and security groups on EC2
  • Your share depends on the services you choose: managed services shift more work to AWS
  • Control types: inherited (physical), shared (patching: AWS the infrastructure, you the guest OS), customer-specific

Exam tip: Who can sign in, and what they may do, is always your side of the line.

Regions and Availability Zones

  • A Region is a separate geographic area; you choose the Regions where resources run
  • An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, networking and connectivity inside a Region
  • AZs are far enough apart to avoid shared failures and close enough for fast synchronous replication
  • IAM users, roles and policies are global: defined once for the account, not per Region
  • Region choice can be enforced later with an organization policy

Exam tip: Spreading across AZs protects against a data center failure; choosing a Region is about location, latency and rules.

Protect the Root User Beyond the guide

  • The root user is created with the account and has complete access, including billing
  • Do not use it for daily work: create an administrative user instead
  • Turn on MFA: up to eight MFA devices, and a phishing-resistant type where possible
  • Never create access keys for the root user
  • Use a strong, unique password and a group email address; restrict who can recover it
  • Monitor root sign-ins, and in Organizations remove root credentials from member accounts

Exam tip: The root user: MFA on, no access keys, locked away, used only for the few tasks that need it.

IAM Users, Groups and Roles

Identity What it is Credentials Use it for
IAM user A person or application identity in one account Long-term: password, access keys Rare cases that cannot use roles or federation
IAM group A collection of IAM users None of its own Giving the same permissions to many users
IAM role An identity that anyone authorized can assume Temporary, from AWS STS Workloads, federated staff, cross-account access
  • Best practice: temporary credentials for people and workloads

Exam tip: When a question offers a user with keys or a role, the role is usually the secure answer.

IAM Policy Types

Policy type Attached to What it does
Identity-based A user, group or role Grants permissions
Resource-based A resource, such as a bucket or queue Grants permissions to named principals, even in other accounts
Permissions boundary A user or role Sets the maximum; grants nothing
Service control policy An organization, OU or account Sets the maximum for member accounts; grants nothing
Session policy A role session Limits that one session

Exam tip: Only identity-based and resource-based policies grant; the rest only limit.

Policy Evaluation: An Explicit Deny Always Wins

  • By default every request is denied
  • An explicit deny in any applicable policy always wins
  • Same account: identity-based and resource-based permissions combine; one allow is enough
  • Boundary and SCP: the identity policy, boundary and SCP must all allow
  • Cross-account: the caller's account and the resource's account must both allow

Exam tip: If one policy says Deny and another says Allow, the answer is Deny.

Least Privilege and IAM Best Practices

  • Least privilege: only the actions, resources and conditions the job needs
  • Start with AWS managed policies, then move to customer managed policies that fit the job
  • IAM Access Analyzer: generates policies from CloudTrail activity, validates policies and finds public and cross-account access
  • Remove unused users, roles, permissions and credentials, using last accessed information
  • Use conditions, such as requiring MFA or TLS
  • Use permissions boundaries to delegate permission management safely

Exam tip: Least privilege is the narrowest policy that still lets the job work.

IAM Roles and Temporary Credentials with AWS STS

  • A role has no password or access keys; assuming it returns temporary credentials from AWS STS
  • Every role has two kinds of policy: a trust policy (who may assume it) and permissions policies (what it may do)
  • AssumeRole: users or roles, in the same or another account
  • AssumeRoleWithSAML and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity: federated users from an identity provider
  • EC2, Lambda and other compute services receive their role's credentials automatically
  • Outside AWS, IAM Roles Anywhere uses X.509 certificates

Exam tip: Applications on AWS get a role; they never carry stored access keys.

Cross-Account Access with Roles

  • Production creates a role whose trust policy names the development account
  • Development lets a group call sts:AssumeRole on that role
  • The developer switches role in the console or calls AssumeRole; STS checks the trust policy and returns temporary credentials
  • While in the role, only the role's permissions apply; the user's own are suspended
  • Add MFA to the role, and audit with CloudTrail

Exam tip: Cross-account access needs two sides: a trust policy in one account and a permission to assume in the other.

Resource-Based Policy or Role?

Assume a role Resource-based policy
Set up A role in the account that owns the resource A policy on the resource names the other account's principals
Caller's own permissions Suspended while in the role Kept: the caller does not switch
Best for Many resources, or temporary elevated access One shared resource: a bucket, queue, topic or key
Limit Works for all access Only services that support resource policies

Exam tip: One resource shared with another account: resource-based policy. Broader access: a role.

Federation with IAM Identity Center Old name

  • AWS IAM Identity Center (old name: AWS Single Sign-On) connects workforce users to AWS accounts and AWS managed applications
  • Identity sources: its own directory, Active Directory, or an external identity provider
  • One point of federation: one SAML 2.0 certificate to manage
  • Permission sets are permissions you define once, provision into accounts and assign to users and groups
  • The organization instance, in the management account, is the best practice and the only type that manages account access
  • Users sign in through the AWS access portal

Exam tip: Staff who already have identities: federate with Identity Center. Customers of your application: Cognito, in the next module.

AWS Directory Service Options [Verify live]

Option What it is Choose it when
AWS Managed Microsoft AD A real Windows Server Active Directory run by AWS You need actual AD features, RDS for SQL Server, or LDAP for Linux
AD Connector A proxy to your on-premises AD; no sync, no copy On-premises users must sign in to AWS with their own credentials
Simple AD A Samba 4 compatible directory; no MFA, no trusts Low-scale, low-cost, basic AD needs
Amazon Cognito A directory for customers of your applications SaaS or web apps with social sign-in
  • As of 5 November 2026: the page also lists a Hybrid Edition to extend self-managed AD; check editions

Exam tip: Existing on-premises directory, no copy: AD Connector. Real Active Directory in AWS: Managed Microsoft AD.

3Multiple accounts, governance and practice

Multiple Accounts with AWS Organizations

  • Use separate accounts to isolate workloads, such as development, test and production
  • AWS Organizations has one management account, many member accounts, and organizational units (OUs) that group them
  • Policies attached to the root, an OU or an account flow down; an account gets only what every parent allows
  • Consolidated billing gives one bill across the organization
  • Run no workloads in the management account: SCPs do not restrict it
  • People use IAM Identity Center; shared services use RAM

Exam tip: New requirement for isolation between environments: separate accounts under Organizations.

Service Control Policies: Guardrails, Not Grants

  • SCPs set the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts; they never grant
  • Effective permissions = what the SCP and the identity or resource policy both allow
  • SCPs do not restrict the management account or service-linked roles; they do restrict a member account's root user
  • Keep FullAWSAccess and add Deny statements, or replace it with an allow list; removing it alone blocks everything
  • Test on an OU first, not on the organization root

Exam tip: An SCP caps what an account can do; it never gives anyone access.

AWS Control Tower and AWS RAM

Service What it does Key terms
AWS Control Tower Sets up and governs a multi-account environment by orchestrating Organizations, Service Catalog and IAM Identity Center Landing zone, controls (preventive, detective, proactive), Account Factory, dashboard
AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) Share a resource you own with accounts, OUs, an organization, or (for some types) IAM roles and users Resource share, VPC subnets, no extra charge; owner keeps ownership

Exam tip: Standard multi-account setup with guardrails: Control Tower. Share instead of copy: RAM.

What the Exam Asks: Secure Access

  • Which identity: root user, IAM user, group or role
  • Which policy type: identity-based, resource-based, boundary, SCP or session
  • Which access path: role, resource-based policy or RAM
  • Which sign-in model: IAM Identity Center, a SAML provider, or a directory option
  • Which multi-account tool: Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower or RAM

Exam tip: Name the identity and the account boundary first, then pick the tool.

Design Check: Lantern and Loom Opens the Doors

Requirement Design
The founder signs in as root every day MFA on root, no access keys, an administrative user for daily work
Web servers must read images from S3 An IAM role on the instances, no stored keys
Developers must update production briefly A cross-account role that trusts the dev account, with MFA
A partner studio uploads to one bucket A bucket policy naming the studio's account
Staff in an existing identity provider need every account IAM Identity Center with permission sets
No account may use an unapproved Region An SCP on the OU
New accounts with built-in guardrails AWS Control Tower
Other accounts must use one VPC subnet AWS RAM
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's responsibility?

  • AControlling physical access to AWS data centers
  • BReplacing failed hardware in an AWS Region
  • CChoosing which IAM permissions its users get
  • DMaintaining the cabling between Availability Zones
Show the answer

Answer: C. Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: their data, identities and permissions. AWS is responsible for the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run its services.

S2Lantern and Loom's founder signs in as the root user for daily work and shares the password with the team. Which TWO actions fix this? (Select TWO.)

  • ATurn on MFA for the root user and store its credentials securely
  • BCreate access keys for the root user for the team's CLI use
  • CKeep the root password in a shared team chat for emergencies
  • DCreate an administrative user for daily work and stop using root
  • EAdd the root user to an IAM group that has a narrower policy
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Protect the root user with MFA and locked-away credentials, and do daily work with an administrative identity. Root access keys and a shared password raise exposure, and an IAM group holds IAM users, not the root user.

S3A user's identity-based policy allows s3:DeleteObject on a bucket. A service control policy on the user's OU explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject. What is the result?

  • AAllowed, because the identity-based policy grants the action
  • BDenied, because an explicit deny overrides any allow
  • CAllowed, because SCPs apply only to the management account
  • DAllowed, if the user also has a permissions boundary
Show the answer

Answer: B. An explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides every allow. SCPs affect the member accounts, not the management account, and a permissions boundary can only limit, never override a deny.

S4Lantern and Loom's web servers on Amazon EC2 must read product images from an Amazon S3 bucket. Which approach is the most secure?

  • AStore an IAM user's access keys in the application configuration file
  • BCreate one shared IAM user for all servers and change its password monthly
  • CBuild the founder's access keys into the server image
  • DAttach an IAM role with S3 read permissions to the instances
Show the answer

Answer: D. A role delivers temporary credentials to the instance automatically, so no long-term keys are stored. Stored keys and shared users can leak and must be rotated by hand.

S5Developers in Lantern and Loom's development account occasionally update objects in a production bucket. The team wants no IAM users in production and a full audit trail. What should the architect do?

  • ACreate a role in production that trusts the dev account, then let developers assume it
  • BCreate an IAM user in production for every developer and give each one a password
  • CShare one production administrator login among the developers and log its use
  • DCopy the production bucket to the dev account and sync the changes back nightly
Show the answer

Answer: A. The production account creates a role with a trust policy naming the development account; developers assume it through STS and receive temporary credentials, and CloudTrail records each AssumeRole call. IAM users and shared logins add long-term credentials.

S6A partner photo studio, in its own AWS account, must upload photos to one S3 bucket owned by Lantern and Loom. The studio's staff should keep working in their own account without switching roles. What is the simplest design?

  • ACreate an IAM user for each photographer in the Lantern and Loom account
  • BShare the Lantern and Loom root credentials with the studio
  • CAdd a bucket policy that allows the studio's account to put objects
  • DMove the bucket into the studio's account
Show the answer

Answer: C. A resource-based policy on the bucket names the other account, so its principals keep their own identities and need an allow in their own account too. Extra IAM users, shared root credentials and moving the bucket do not meet the need.

S7Which TWO statements about service control policies (SCPs) are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • ASCPs grant permissions to the IAM users in member accounts
  • BSCPs set the maximum permissions available in member accounts
  • CSCPs restrict the users and roles in the management account
  • DSCPs do not apply to the root user of a member account
  • ESCPs do not restrict the management account
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. SCPs only set limits and never grant, and they affect member accounts, including a member account's root user, but not the management account.

S8Lantern and Loom has several AWS accounts. Its engineers already sign in with accounts in an external SAML identity provider. The team wants single sign-on to every account, with permissions managed in one place. Which service fits?

  • AA separate IAM user for each engineer in every account
  • BAWS IAM Identity Center with permission sets
  • CAmazon Cognito user pools shared by all engineers
  • DAWS Resource Access Manager with shared roles
Show the answer

Answer: B. IAM Identity Center connects an external identity provider, provisions permission sets into the accounts of an organization and gives one portal for sign-in. Cognito is for application customers, and RAM shares resources, not roles.

S9A company wants employees to sign in to AWS applications and the console with their existing on-premises Active Directory credentials, without copying directory data into AWS. Which AWS Directory Service option fits?

  • AAWS Managed Microsoft AD as a new standalone directory
  • BSimple AD with a one-time user import
  • CAmazon Cognito user pools with imported users
  • DAD Connector as a proxy to the on-premises directory
Show the answer

Answer: D. AD Connector forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises domain controllers, with no directory synchronization. Managed Microsoft AD, Simple AD and Cognito hold directory data in AWS.

S10Lantern and Loom is adding accounts for development, test and production. Leaders want a fast standard setup with built-in guardrails, self-service account creation and a dashboard of compliance status. Which service should the architect choose?

  • AAWS Control Tower
  • BAWS Resource Access Manager
  • CAWS Directory Service
  • DIAM groups in the management account
Show the answer

Answer: A. Control Tower sets up a landing zone, applies controls, offers Account Factory for self-service accounts and shows a dashboard. RAM shares resources, Directory Service provides directories, and IAM groups do not govern accounts.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Responsibility AWS secures the cloud; you secure identities, data and settings in it
Root and users root with MFA and no keys; roles and temporary credentials over users with keys
Policies only identity-based and resource-based grant; an explicit deny always wins
Access paths assume a role across accounts; use a resource policy to share one resource
Many accounts Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower, RAM, IAM Identity Center and the right directory
